questions.prompt: The ALU is the part of the datapath that
options: Performs arithmetic and logic on operand bits
Chooses which process runs next
Translates C into assembly
Stores files
questions.explanation: Add, subtract, AND, OR, and the related flags are ALU work. Scheduling and compiling happen in software.

options: MAR holds an address; MDR holds the data word being transferred
MAR holds data; MDR holds the opcode name as text
Both registers hold only cache tags
MAR is the program counter and MDR is the stack pointer
questions.explanation: The memory address register names the location. The memory data register holds the word moving to or from that location.
traps: Swapping MAR and MDR swaps the whole story.

questions.prompt: The control unit’s job is to
options: Turn a decoded opcode into control signals for the datapath
Store the user’s files
Replace the clock
Allocate disk blocks
questions.explanation: The datapath can add, move, and store. The control unit decides which of those actions happen on this cycle.

questions.prompt: Which pieces sit on the CPU datapath?
options: ALU
Register file
Compiler
Buses between the registers
questions.explanation: The datapath is the hardware that holds and moves operand bits. A compiler is a program that runs before those bits exist.

questions.prompt: A processor averages 2 cycles per instruction. Which reading is fair?
options: An instruction can take more than one clock
The clock is unused half the time, so CPI must be 0.5
Every instruction finishes in half a cycle
CPI is the cache block size
questions.explanation: CPI counts clocks per instruction. Multi-cycle instructions, stalls, and cache misses all push the average above 1.
traps: Inverting CPI into “instructions per cycle” without saying so.

questions.prompt: After a successful fetch, the instruction register holds
options: The instruction that was just read from memory
The address of the previous instruction only
Only the condition flags
The page table
questions.explanation: Fetch copies the memory word into the IR. The program counter holds an address, not the instruction bits.

questions.prompt: A simple fetch copies PC into MAR, reads memory into IR, then increments PC before execute. Why increment so early?
options: The sequential successor is ready, and a branch can still overwrite PC during execute
The ALU can run only when PC is even
The increment erases the instruction from memory
MAR and PC must stay equal forever
questions.explanation: The common case is “fall through”. Execute overwrites PC when the instruction is a taken branch; otherwise the next fetch uses the incremented value.
traps: Thinking the PC increments only after the whole instruction, so a branch has nowhere to write.

questions.prompt: Which register is deliberately not a general-purpose data register?
options: The program counter
A register that ADD can name as a destination
A register that MOV can name as a source
There is no difference: every register is general-purpose
questions.explanation: The PC is a register, but ordinary arithmetic does not use it as scratch storage. It exists to name the next instruction.

questions.prompt: In one or two sentences, what is the difference between the datapath and the control unit?
questions.answer: The datapath holds and transforms bits. The control unit decides which transformation happens on this cycle.
questions.explanation: Opcode bits and flags feed the control unit. Its output is a bundle of select and enable signals into the datapath.
